title: Book review: C. A. Floudas and P. M. Pardalos (eds.), State of the Art in Global Optimization. Computational Methods and Applications
contribution: A short, uncritical Optima review of the proceedings of the 1995 Princeton global-optimization conference (36 refereed papers). As reviewer, Sahinidis singles out six contributions: two on finiteness, one of them his own with Shectman, and one on range reduction.
problem_entry: n/a (book review): a descriptive notice of the seventh volume of Kluwer's Nonconvex Optimization and Its Applications series (p. 12).
key_idea: The reviewer's selection (p. 12): Horst-van Thoai finiteness by integral branching, all QAPLIB problems with n <= 15 solved by branch and bound, Kearfott's interval branch and bound, Van Voorhis-Al-Khayyal range reduction for QCQP, Shectman-Sahinidis finiteness by exhaustiveness plus incumbent branching; plus Tuy's d.c. location problems (p. 13).
experiments: none (relays one computational claim: all QAPLIB problems with n <= 15 solved, p. 12)
positioning: Praises the volume and the series without criticism; one of the six highlighted contributions is his own (pp. 12-13).
writing: One sentence per highlighted paper naming the observation that makes it work; the remaining papers listed by authors only, then topic and application lists (pp. 12-13).
limits_future: n/a: no limitations or open problems named; ends by agreeing with the editors' praise (p. 13).

method_links.note: Weak: one of the six contributions he chose to describe is range reduction used to accelerate QCQP branch and bound. This is a reviewer's selection, not a method statement.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: finite branching by exhaustiveness plus incumbent branching
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: His own paper with Shectman is summarized by this finiteness result. The same rule is restated in S058 pp. 8-9 and S077 p. 24; all are restatements of one result, not independent evidence.

transferable: When summarizing prior results in a review or related-work section, give each one in a sentence that names the observation that makes it work (e.g., the problems can be viewed as integer programs, so integral branching gives finiteness) (p. 12).

quotes.text: The key observation is that the underlying problems can be viewed as integer programs. Finiteness can, therefore, be achieved by integral branching.

J.P. Shectman and N.V. Sahinidis prove that exhaustiveness and branching on the incumbent whenever possible in tandem ensure finiteness of rectangular-subdivision-based branch and bound algorithms for global minimization if separable concave programs.

title: Globally optimal robust process control
contribution: Poses robust controller synthesis against nonlinear time-varying perturbations as a BMI-constrained optimization and solves it globally by branch and bound with LMI bounds built from McCormick envelopes. The design is about 50% less conservative than DK-iteration on a benchmark, and a 48-state reactive-ion-etcher instance is solved.
problem_entry: DK-iteration alternates on a nonconvex problem and can give conservative designs even for small processes; earlier global BMI methods need iterated nonconvex feasibility problems or scale badly with the number of uncertainties (p. 1).
key_idea: Write the design directly as a BMI optimization (eqs. 9-13, p. 3) and branch on it. Lower bound: an LMI with each bilinear product replaced by an interval-bounded variable plus McCormick inequalities. Upper bound: an LMI with some variables fixed. Variable bounds from auxiliary LMIs (eqs. 15-19, p. 4).
assumptions: Norm-bounded nonlinear time-varying block-diagonal perturbations with constant scalings (pp. 2-3); unrestricted controller order (p. 7); Pade delay approximation covered by the uncertainty weights (p. 7); branch and bound needs a relaxation whose gap does not grow as regions shrink, globally solvable convex relaxations and lowest-bound node selection (p. 4).
proof_devices: McCormick envelopes of bilinear terms embedded in an LMI relaxation, so each node bound is a polynomial-time convex problem (eqs. 15-18, p. 4)
LMI upper bound by fixing a subset of the variables (eq. 19, p. 4)
variable ranges computed by auxiliary LMIs (p. 4, citing Yamada et al. [15])
BMI NP-hardness asserted as straightforward, not proved (p. 2); convergence by citation of Ryoo and Sahinidis 1996 (p. 4)
experiments: Mass-spring benchmark: about 50% less conservative than DK- and LR-iteration, order-4 controller (p. 5); cited adhesive coater only about 10% (p. 6); 48-state reactive ion etcher: performance value 0.9834 < 1, order-48 controller, set-point response more than twice as fast as a published LQ design (pp. 7-8); no CPU times, node counts, tolerances or hardware reported.
positioning: Against DK-iteration (ad hoc, conservative) and two earlier global BMI algorithms; claims tighter bounds and a more direct approach but compares only with DK- and LR-iteration (pp. 1, 4-6).
writing: Short application paper; claims the largest BMI control problem solved to date in the introduction and in section 7 (pp. 1, 7).
limits_future: Concludes that global optimality matters for nonconservative controllers and that processes of moderate dimension are within reach (p. 8); reduced-order robust controllers, a harder nonconvex problem, are left aside (p. 7).

method_links.note: Range reduction is stated as the key to tight bounding, and each variable's bounds are computed by an LMI. The device is borrowed from Yamada et al., not the duality-based test.
The node relaxation is an LMI (semidefinite) problem, chosen because it is polynomial-time solvable. No time or failure accounting is reported, so bound per second is not measured.
The certified global design is the yardstick for the field's standard heuristic (DK/LR-iteration), but on one benchmark plus one cited case rather than a library. The weaker 10% case is reported too.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: price of local search on the literature's own instances
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Re-solves the published mass-spring benchmark to global optimality and reports how conservative the DK- and LR-iteration designs are; the same move appears in S058 pp. 13-15.

transferable: When a field's standard method alternates between two convex subproblems, write the joint problem with its bilinear coupling and branch on it. Relax each product by McCormick inequalities inside the field's native convex class (here LMIs), so every node bound stays a polynomial-time convex problem (pp. 3-4).
Report the case where the incumbent heuristic is close (about 10%) next to the one where it is far off (about 50%) (pp. 5-6).
coauthors: Jeremy G. VanAntwerp, Richard D. Braatz (corresponding author)

quotes.text: Reducing the ranges of all problem variable as much as possible is frequently a key to tight objective function bounding.
We would like to point out that the iterative methods do not always perform so poorly.

coauthors: n/a (roster; the Scholar entry lists committee members as authors)

title: Applications of global optimization to process and molecular design
contribution: Reviews two group applications to show the value of certified global optima. On nine literature JIT-flowshop instances, BARON's global designs save 11-26% (average 17%) over direct-pattern-search designs. On a refrigerant-design MINLP (an R12 replacement), it ranks 28 designs. Range reduction, finite branching and convex extensions are named as what made the solves possible (read as the 22 Feb 2000 preprint).
problem_entry: Show with concrete examples that identifying global optima of MINLP formulations matters in practice; both problems had been attacked with local search before (abstract, p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: No new method. BARON's keys are duality- and feasibility-based range reduction, finite branching schemes and convex extensions of nonlinear functions of 0-1 variables (pp. 4-10). Range reduction is presented as cheap approximations of the 2n bound-tightening LPs (pp. 5-8).
assumptions: JIT: convex objective and linear constraints, integrality the only nonconvexity, four degrees of freedom (p. 13). Refrigerant: Joback-Stephanopoulos group contributions, structural constraints from [33], 44 groups, finite bounds on all variables (pp. 15-23). The property estimates are admitted to be uncertain (p. 22).
proof_devices: value-function and supporting-hyperplane argument giving x_j >= x_j^U - (U - L)/lambda_j (pp. 6-7; Table 1, p. 8)
feasibility-based tightening as poor man's linear programs looped over the variables (p. 6)
finite vs epsilon-finite termination; periodic bisection for exhaustiveness and branching at the incumbent (pp. 8-9)
convex-extension theory stated as four numbered results without proofs (pp. 9-10)
experiments: JIT: 9 literature instances, global designs vs direct pattern search, savings 11-26% (average 17%) (pp. 13-15); refrigerant MINLP (48 integer, 14 binary, 21 continuous variables, 64 constraints), base case solved in about 1 CPU minute and 2570 nodes on a 332 MHz RS/6000, 28 ranked designs (pp. 24-25).
positioning: Earlier molecular-design work by many groups, including genetic-algorithm, simulated-annealing and stochastic methods, is classed as search that is only local in nature (pp. 15, 22, 28-30).
writing: Framed as two global-optimization success stories (abstract, p. 1); branch and bound explained with a one-variable picture for non-specialists (pp. 3-4); theory listed without proofs (pp. 9-10).
limits_future: Stability of the novel molecules is open (p. 24); larger savings for larger problems asserted but not tested (p. 15); the claim that the MINLP was unsolvable without the devices is not backed by a reported run (p. 24).

method_links.note: Range reduction comes first among BARON's keys to success and is restated with its formulas. The refrigerant MINLP could not be solved without range reduction, branching rules and relaxation rules; these are bundled, so this is not an ablation of reduction alone.
Weak: both applications run on BARON and the paper describes the code's components; the applications come from group projects ([12], [33]).
The certified optimum is the yardstick for the literature's heuristic designs, but on nine small instances and one molecular benchmark, with no library or portfolio conclusion.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: price of local search on the literature's own instances
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Re-solves nine published JIT instances with the literature's parameters and tabulates per-instance savings, split by cost term, against the published pattern-search designs; also S079 pp. 5-6.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: ranked near-global list via integer cuts under model uncertainty
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Because the property estimates are uncertain, an algorithm that guarantees global optimality is re-run with integer cuts excluding the earlier solutions to list non-global designs; 28 designs are ranked.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: finite branching by exhaustiveness plus incumbent branching
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Claims that finite algorithms are faster than convergent ones even at a positive tolerance, and gives branching-point rules for finiteness (restating Shectman and Sahinidis 1998).

transferable: Re-solve the literature's own instances, with its parameters, to certified optimality and tabulate per-instance savings split by cost term, so the reader sees where the local method lost (Tables 3-5, pp. 14-15).

When the model's coefficients are estimates (group contributions), return a ranked list of global and near-global designs by re-solving with integer cuts that exclude every earlier solution (p. 22; Table 8, p. 25).
Branching-point rule: bisect every few iterations for exhaustiveness, branch at the incumbent when it lies in the node (it becomes gapless), else at the relaxation solution (p. 9).

quotes.text: Although [33] uses an algorithm that guarantees global optimality, we still obtain several non-global solutions to the problem in order to alleviate the difficulty due to uncertainty in the thermodynamic property estimation techniques that were used.
Without the range reduction, branching rules, and relaxation construction rules described in Section 2, we were unable to solve this MINLP model.

title: BARON—Branch and reduce optimization navigator
contribution: The BARON 4.0 user's manual (revision of 28 June 2000) documents branch and reduce: marginals, probing and poor man's LP range reduction on every node, McCormick-based factorable relaxations and finiteness-oriented branching. It also documents a callable core with seven user exits, 11 specialized modules plus a factorable NLP module, a default for every option and a dated version history.
problem_entry: Nonconvex problems with multiple local optima across engineering; BARON as a system for solving them to global optimality, combining interval analysis and duality in the reduce step with branch and bound (p. 7); each version tied to applications (pp. 7-8).
key_idea: Range-reduction tests on every node in pre- and post-processing; the node is re-solved while reduction is significant, then branched (pp. 19-21, 50). Devices: marginals and probing (pp. 12-17), poor man's LPs (pp. 17-19), factorable relaxations (pp. 20-24), and violation-based branching with periodic bisection, incumbent branching and omega-branching (p. 24).
assumptions: Relaxation gap nonincreasing as regions shrink (p. 11). Duality-based tests need a convex relaxation solved with duals, so the user's lower-bounding routine must return marginals and build underestimators from the current bounds (pp. 20, 59). Factorable functions are limited to exp, ln, x^alpha, beta^x (p. 41). Variable bounds are optional in the parser (p. 100), though relaxation tightness depends on bounds (p. 20). The user picks the feasibility tolerance (p. 59).
proof_devices: value-function and supporting-hyperplane derivation of the marginals rule kappa_j = x_j^U - (U - L)/lambda_j (pp. 12, 15)
probing: fix a variable at a bound, re-solve the relaxation, intersect the linear underestimator of the value function with the incumbent level (p. 15; Table 2.2, p. 17)
pathological two-variable case for poor man's LPs, with the argument that solving the 2n LPs once at the root keeps a nonredundant bound in every later subdomain (pp. 18-19)
tangent-point equation for the convex envelope of an odd monomial over an interval containing zero (p. 24)
experiments: Worked examples only. On x1x2 <= 4: 5 iterations with a separable relaxation, solved at the root with McCormick or with marginals plus probing, 3 vs 5 nodes with incumbent branching (pp. 25-31). A Floudas-Pardalos concave QP: 17 iterations with bisection branch and bound vs 7 with branch and reduce (p. 32). Toy-instance module logs (Chapter 8).
positioning: n/a (manual); references are mostly the group's own papers, McCormick, the Floudas-Pardalos test collection and subsolver manuals (pp. 103-105).
writing: Manual voice; each device shown with a figure and a worked example with node counts (pp. 12-35); every option listed with a default, and users told they need not change any (p. 46).
limits_future: The general factorable module does not exploit the structure the specialized modules use (p. 41); UNIX only (p. 42); fractional module only under OSL and MISDP only with SDPA, more interfaces planned (p. 43); no warranty, free for non-commercial use (p. 8).

method_links.note: Reduction runs on every node in pre- and post-processing, and the node is re-solved after significant reduction. Cheap reductions are on and probing is off by default. Worked examples: 17 vs 7 iterations, and a root-node proof with a weak relaxation. This is a full-text statement of the marginals rule that SKILL.md cites only via later restatements.

Dated version history with code sizes, from 1,800 GAMS lines to about 26,000 lines of FORTRAN 90 and 17,000 of C, each version taking in group techniques and applications; 17 students credited with shaping, developing and testing the ideas in the code. Naming caveat: the GAMS code is the first version, while Version 1.0 is dated 2 March 1995.
The version-4 factorable NLP module allows an entirely LP-based approach and uses an LP relaxation by default; a per-component CPU-time breakdown is written by default.
The IQP module defaults to a quadratic relaxation, and a mixed-integer SDP module ships with SDPA, so in 2000 nonlinear relaxations were defaults inside specialized modules.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The times option, on by default, writes a breakdown of CPU time by section; every log splits time into preprocessing, navigating, relaxed, local, tightening, marginals and probing.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: finite branching by exhaustiveness plus incumbent branching
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Periodic bisection for exhaustiveness and branching at the incumbent are named as keys to finiteness; in the worked example, incumbent branching proves globality in 3 nodes instead of 5.

transferable: Solve the exact 2n bound-tightening LPs once at the root, then use one-constraint interval propagation (poor man's LPs) at the nodes; the root step protects the cheap test from its pathological case (pp. 18-19, 52).
After a node's relaxation, run reduction and re-solve the same node, before branching, while the bound improves by more than a set tolerance, up to a pass limit (pp. 21, 50).

Print a CPU-time breakdown by component (preprocessing, relaxation, local search, tightening, marginals, probing) with every run, so the cost of each device is visible without a profiler (pp. 51, 65-66).
In a tutorial example, use the weaker relaxation on purpose so each acceleration shows in the node count, then show the strong relaxation closing the gap at the root (pp. 26, 30-31).

Build the solver as a core with user exits for range reduction, lower bounding, feasibility checking, starting points, branching, local search and objective evaluation, so a new problem class can be prototyped on the same engine (pp. 55-61).
coauthors: none (sole author; 17 students and two NYU colleagues acknowledged, pp. 8-9)

quotes.text: These tests are applied to every subproblem of the search tree in pre- and post-processing steps to contract the search space and reduce the relaxation gap.

In this way, the capabilities of this module subsume those of all other specialized modules. However, this module is not designed to fully exploit the special structure of the problems addressed by the above-described specialized modules.
